TFSA over-contribution: how the 1% monthly tax is counted, why putting money back too soon triggers it, and what taking it out fixes

Follow the Income Tax Act’s excess TFSA amount month by month: why a withdrawal does not free room until 1 January, how the 1% tax on the highest excess adds up, what removing the excess costs and saves, and what CRA’s 2024 statistics say about who is exposed.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Price a TFSA over-contribution: the 1% monthly tax, when to take the excess out, and what 1 January fixes

The July 2026 contribution creates an excess of $5,000. The tax is 1% of the highest excess in each month it exists: 4 months here, $200.00 for 2026. Withdrawing $5,000 in October 2026 ends it, but that month is still taxed because the excess existed in it. A TFSA return (RC243) is due by 30 June of the year after each year with tax.

The central idea

A TFSA withdrawal gives its room back only on 1 January of the next year. Put the money back before then without other room and the amount over is an excess TFSA amount, taxed at 1% of the highest excess in every month it exists, including the month you take it out. There is no CAD 2,000 cushion as with an RRSP. Withdrawing the excess stops the tax and loses no room, because that withdrawal also comes back on 1 January. Waiting for January can cost less when the excess is small and the year is nearly over, but each month adds 1% of the excess. In 2024, 5.69 million of 19.32 million TFSA holders made a withdrawal.

01

The usual way people over-contribute

Few people set out to put too much into a tax-free savings account (TFSA). The common path is ordinary: you fill your room in January, take some money out in spring for a car repair or a trip that is then cancelled, and put it back in summer. If you had no other room, that second deposit is an over-contribution, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) charges 1% a month on it until it is gone.

The questions are practical: how is the tax counted, when does it stop, is it better to withdraw the excess now or wait for 1 January, and does taking it out cost any room? The calculator follows the rules in the Income Tax Act month by month for 2026 and 2027.

02

What counts as an excess, in the Act’s own terms

Section 207.01(1) of the Income Tax Act defines your excess TFSA amount at any moment in a year as A − B − C − D − E, if positive:

ElementMeaning
AContributions made so far this year (other than transfers between your own TFSAs and exempt survivor contributions)
BUnused room at the end of last year
CWithdrawals made last year
DThis year’s TFSA dollar limit, if you were resident in Canada at any time in the year
EThe qualifying portion of withdrawals made so far this year

B + C + D is the room on 1 January that CRA shows you. The key is E. The qualifying portion of a withdrawal is the lesser of the withdrawal and the excess just before it. A withdrawal made while you have no excess has a qualifying portion of nil, so it does nothing to offset a deposit later in the same year. Its room only comes back through C, next year. CRA’s contribution room page puts it the same way: withdrawals are regained as room on 1 January of the following year.

Section 207.02 then sets the tax: if you have an excess at any time in a calendar month, you pay 1% of the highest such amount in that month. Three consequences follow:

  • There is no grace amount. The RRSP’s CAD 2,000 cushion, explained in the RRSP room ledger guide, has no TFSA counterpart; the tax applies from the first dollar.
  • Part months count in full. An excess created on the 30th, or removed on the 2nd, still makes that month taxable at 1% of the highest amount reached.
  • The tax is not prorated or compounded. It is simply 1% of each month’s peak, added up.

03

Four worked cases

The first three use the calculator’s default: CAD 7,000 of room on 1 January 2026, a CAD 7,000 deposit in January, a CAD 5,000 withdrawal in March and CAD 5,000 put back in July. The 2027 dollar limit is assumed to be CAD 7,000.

  1. Taken out in October (the default). The July deposit makes A = CAD 12,000 against room of CAD 7,000; the March withdrawal had no excess to reduce, so E is nil and the excess is CAD 5,000. July, August, September and October are taxed: 4 × CAD 50 = CAD 200. Withdrawing CAD 5,000 in October is a qualifying portion and ends the excess, but October still counts.
  2. Taken out in July, as soon as it is noticed. One month: CAD 50.
  3. Left in until January. July to December: 6 × CAD 50 = CAD 300. On 1 January 2027 the room is CAD 7,000 − CAD 12,000 + CAD 5,000 of 2026 withdrawals + CAD 7,000 = CAD 7,000, which is positive, so the excess is gone and nothing is owed for 2027.
  4. A misread room figure, with no withdrawal. Someone with CAD 7,000 of room deposits CAD 17,000 in January. The excess is CAD 10,000: CAD 100 a month, CAD 1,200 for 2026 if left in. On 1 January 2027 the room is CAD 7,000 − CAD 17,000 + CAD 7,000 = −CAD 3,000, so CAD 3,000 is still over for all of 2027: another CAD 360. Withdrawing the CAD 10,000 in March instead would have cost CAD 300.

The second chart tracks your inputs month by month. The third repeats them with every possible removal month. The fourth shows what is in the account and what room is left on 1 January 2027 under four choices.

04

Taking the excess out loses no room

A common worry is that withdrawing the excess wastes room. It does not. A withdrawal of the excess is counted twice in your favour: its qualifying portion cancels the excess this year (element E), and the whole withdrawal is added back as room next January (element C).

In the default case, the net amount in the TFSA plus the room on 1 January 2027 is CAD 14,000 in every version: CAD 2,000 in the account and CAD 12,000 of room if you remove the excess or wait to re-deposit, or CAD 7,000 and CAD 7,000 if you leave it in. The fourth chart shows this for your own inputs. The only real difference is the tax, plus any tax on income earned on the excess.

The one thing a withdrawal cannot do is offset a later deposit in the same year if it was made while there was no excess. CRA’s cancelled RC4466 guide, still online, gives exactly this case: someone over by CAD 2,000 withdraws CAD 3,700; only CAD 2,000 is a qualifying portion, and a CAD 1,000 deposit two months later creates a new CAD 1,000 excess even though more was taken out than was needed. The extra CAD 1,700 comes back as room the next January.

05

Withdraw now, or wait for 1 January?

The cost of waiting is simple: 1% of the excess for each extra month, which the third chart shows as a straight staircase. Against it, leaving the money in keeps it invested tax-free and saves a withdrawal and re-deposit. A 1% monthly charge is about 12% a year, far more than most investments can be expected to earn over a few months, so removing the excess promptly is usually the cheaper path. The exception is an excess found in December: that month is taxed either way, and the room returning on 1 January may absorb it with no further tax.

Two cautions. First, 1 January only clears the excess if the room returning (last year’s withdrawals plus the new dollar limit) is larger; a large over-deposit like case 4 continues into the new year. Second, the 2027 dollar limit had not been announced when this guide was reviewed. Under section 207.01(1) it is CAD 5,000 indexed to inflation and rounded to the nearest CAD 500; the dollar-limit indexation guide explains the rounding. Enter the announced figure once CRA publishes it.

06

Who is exposed

CRA’s TFSA statistics for the 2024 tax year (page dated 30 April 2026) count 19,322,830 TFSA holders. Of them, 10,979,910 contributed, 5,685,240 made at least one withdrawal and 1,711,020 maximized their contributions, in CRA’s wording. Holders made 31.9 million withdrawals totalling about CAD 69.9 billion, and 174.6 million contributions totalling about CAD 123.5 billion.

Younger holders withdraw more often, while older holders more often fill their room; both groups can trip the same-year rule. CRA does not publish the number of people with an excess or the tax collected in these tables, so the chart shows the population exposed, not the number taxed. Counts are individuals, rounded by CRA, and the age is at the end of the tax year.

07

If you have already over-contributed

  1. Withdraw the excess. CRA’s over-contribution page asks you to withdraw it as soon as possible; your financial institution reports the withdrawal to CRA, so you do not need to call.
  2. File Form RC243. When any TFSA tax applies, the TFSA return (RC243) and its Schedule A, which lists your highest excess for each month, are due with payment by 30 June of the following year: 30 June 2027 for 2026. CRA may otherwise assess from issuers’ records and send a notice in summer.
  3. Ask for relief if it was a genuine mistake. CRA can waive or cancel all or part of the tax if it considers it fair, looking at whether the excess arose from a reasonable error and how promptly it was withdrawn. Remove the excess before you ask.
  4. Check your room with your own records. CRA’s room figure is updated only after issuers report, by the end of February for the previous year; deposits and withdrawals made since are not reflected.

08

What the calculator leaves out

  • Growth and income. Amounts are deposits and withdrawals, not market values. Income or gains on an excess can be taxed under the separate advantage rules, especially if an over-contribution is deliberate.
  • Several deposits and withdrawals. The model allows one deposit in January, one withdrawal, one re-deposit and one removal of the full excess. Real accounts may need a full ledger; the same A − B − C − D − E rule applies to each transaction.
  • Transfers, survivors and non-residents. Direct transfers between your own TFSAs are not contributions or withdrawals; exempt survivor contributions and non-resident contributions have their own rules and a separate tax.
  • Late-filing penalties and interest. Not included.
